[title]: <> (Obfuscation (Part II): Diamond iO)
[date]: <> (2026/07/28)
[category]: <> (general)
[pandoc]: <> (--mathjax)

_Special thanks to Sora Suegami and_ _Janmajaya Mall for feedback and review._

In the last part of this series, we went through the full tech tree of the most mainstream and conservative line of cryptographic obfuscation (iO) protocols. These protocols allow you to “encrypt” programs in such a way that anyone can run the “encrypted” program on plaintext inputs and get plaintext outputs, without being able to see the internal logic of the program. This can be used for all kinds of use cases, particularly situations where the program contains some secret key internally, and obfuscating accomplishes the goal of giving someone a package that lets them do *some things* with the secret key *in some circumstances*, but not anything else.

The biggest downside of these protocols so far has been their literally galactic runtime - if you actually try to figure out how long it would take to run one of them, you would get an answer longer than the lifetime of the universe. As a result, despite recent breakthroughs in feasibility, obfuscation protocols have so far been theoretical curiosities.

This post will describe in detail a different style of obfuscation: diamond iO ([paper](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/236), [presentation](https://simons.berkeley.edu/talks/sora-suegami-ethereum-foundation-machina-io-2025-06-24)). This approach relies on much “braver” and more untested cryptographic assumptions, but it achieves having merely “planetary”, rather than galactic runtime - still infeasible today, but perhaps only a few further optimizations away from becoming a reality at least for a few use cases.

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

<small style="text-align: center"><span><em class="select-text pointer-events-auto">Different types of obfuscation</em></span></small>

</center><br>

## How does diamond iO work?

At a high level, diamond iO is built by modifying the BGG+14 attribute-based encryption (ABE) scheme, [explained in the previous post](https://vitalik.eth.limo/general/2026/06/29/obfuscation1.html#attribute-based-encryption-abe). I highly recommend re-reading that section before continuing.

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

<small style="text-align: center"><em class="select-text pointer-events-auto">It’s also not this Abe. Bonus points if you know which Abe this one is - harder than the four in the last post!</em></small>

</center><br>

Like, the more traditional iO protocols, diamond iO runs the computation in FHE inside of ABE, and then gives the evaluator a way to decrypt the result only if it’s actually the outcome of running the computation correctly. But the way that diamond iO _uses_ this machinery is different. First, it uses a completely different mechanism to do conditional FHE decryption. Second, it uses a completely different mechanism to generate the encodings for the input.

These two modifications are connected to each other, and are the real reason why diamond iO manages to be much more efficient - it’s “just as computationally intensive as” functional encryption, instead of being a much more complicated tower on top of FE.

As a reminder, BGG+14 works by maintaining encodings of the form

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * (B - G * m) + e" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * (B - G * m) + e$</span>

Where:

* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> is a secret
* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B$</span> is a public matrix, of which there is a different one for each “wire” in the circuit
* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span> is the bit on that wire during the computation
* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="e" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$e$</span> is an “error”

(alternatively, you can add <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G * m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G * m$</span> instead of subtracting; both give equally valid and efficient schemes)

Given two <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B$</span> matrices representing two “input wires” to an operation - either addition, multiplication or negation - you can generate a <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B$</span> matrix representing the output wire. Given valid encodings for two inputs to an operation, you can get an encoding for the output - <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="1 - m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$1 - m$</span>, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_a + m_b" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_a + m_b$</span> or <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_a * m_b" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_a * m_b$</span> - that is based on the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B$</span> matrix representing the output wire. Importantly, this is not fully-homomorphic encryption: to multiply, you need to know either <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_a" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_a$</span> or <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_b" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_b$</span> in the clear.

In BGG+14, there is a step at the end, which allows decoding a pre-selected output, only if the value in the computation on some “output” wire equals 0. Here, we do not do that. Instead, what we will do is just extract the data that we need from the encoding. But in both cases, the decryption method depends on the encoding being based on a specific matrix <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B_{final}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B_{final}$</span> representing the output wire - this is how we enforce that decryption can happen if you did the computation correctly, but not in any other context.

The core of diamond iO is:

* Generate BGG+14 <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B$</span>\-matrices and encodings representing the input <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="x" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$x$</span>, plus a few other things
* Run a computation, over these BGG+14 encodings, that converts <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="x" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$x$</span> into an *FHE ciphertext* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="FHE.enc(f(x, z))" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$FHE.enc(f(x, z))$</span>, where <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f$</span> is public and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="z" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$z$</span> is an internal hidden input that the obfuscator is trying to hide
* Run another slightly modified BGG+14 step to FHE-decrypt the output
* Finally, do a “trapdoor” step, borrowing similar machinery to BGG+14 decryption but using it in very different ways, to get the result - only in the situation where the circuit that you ran is the “correct” one

The complexity of diamond iO rests in three places:

* What you do to the encoding of the output at the end, that allows this FHE decryption only in situations where the circuit that was computed is exactly the same circuit representing <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f$</span>, and without fully leaking the key
* Some adjustments to <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f(x, z)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f(x, z)$</span> to take into account the fact that this whole scheme is only secure if the outputs of the FHE decryption are fully uniformly distributed random-looking, and then convert it from “obfuscate <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f(x, z)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f(x, z)$</span> hiding <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="z" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$z$</span>” to “full iO that hides the program”
* How to let the evaluator construct the ABE encodings of the inputs, without giving away the secrets.

The first two ideas came from prior work, particularly [HLL23](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/1716) and [AKY24](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1719). The third piece, the mechanism for constructing the ABE encodings of the inputs, originally came from [GGH15](https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/645); the new contribution in diamond iO is to use it not to evaluate the whole program (which turned out insecure) but to generate BGG+ encodings for the inputs.

We will tackle these three pieces in turn.

## The decryption step

Assume for now that the evaluator _somehow_ gets as input four types of BGG+ encodings of:

* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$1$</span> (this will be helpful later, for constructing these encodings)
* FHE encryptions of the fixed hidden input to <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f$</span>, which we denote <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="z" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$z$</span> (we’ll denote the encrypted version <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="E[z]" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$E[z]$</span>)
* The public input bits: <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * (B_{x_1} - x_1 * G) + e_{x_1} … s * (B_{x_L} - x_L * G) + e_{x_L}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * (B_{x_1} - x_1 * G) + e_{x_1} … s * (B_{x_L} - x_L * G) + e_{x_L}$</span>, where <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="x_1 … x_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$x_1 … x_L$</span> is the input to <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f$</span>
* An FHE decryption key (which must be low-norm, and the last value must be -1), which we will call <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t$</span>

We’ll label this ensemble <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="[1, E[z], x, t]" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$[1, E[z], x, t]$</span>.

The evaluator first runs the BGG+ computation using the encodings of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="E[z]" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$E[z]$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="x" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$x$</span>. Remember, the computation is not <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f(x, z)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f(x, z)$</span> directly, rather, it’s <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="FHE.eval(f, x, E[z])" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$FHE.eval(f, x, E[z])$</span>. From the BGG+ perspective, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="x" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$x$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="E[z]" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$E[z]$</span> are both cleartext bits. From the FHE perspective, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="z" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$z$</span> is a hidden input, of which only the encrypted form is known to the evaluator.

At the end of doing the BGG+ computation, the evaluator has BGG+ encodings of bits of the FHE ciphertext representing <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f(x, z)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f(x, z)$</span>.

BGG+ is not fully homomorphic encryption; in general, computing on BGG+ encodings requires having the underlying cleartext. But we can avoid this rule for _additions_, and for _multiplications by known values_. This is because a BGG+ encoding of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_a * m_b" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_a * m_b$</span> is computed via:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="c_{out} = m_b * ​c_a ​+ c_b * ​G^{-1}(B_a)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$c_{out} = m_b * ​c_a ​+ c_b * ​G^{-1}(B_a)$</span>

(If the encodings were *adding* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G * m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G * m$</span> instead of subtracting, then it would be <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G^{-1}(-B_a)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G^{-1}(-B_a)$</span> instead)

We can allow <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_a" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_a$</span> to be unknown (ie. given to us via encodings only), as long as <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_b" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_b$</span> is known.

This is an important fact for us. To see why, remember the structure of GSW decryption (also described in [the previous post in this series](https://vitalik.eth.limo/general/2026/06/29/obfuscation1.html#fully-homomorphic-encryption-fhe)):

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

Because the evaluator knows all the bits of the actual execution trace, including the final FHE ciphertext (which we’ll call <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="Y" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$Y$</span>), we can give the evaluator the FHE decryption key, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t$</span>, only as BGG+ encodings.

Let’s see how the decryption works.

We want to compute <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t * Y" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t * Y$</span>. We have only BGG+ encodings of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t$</span>, and we have both the BGG+ encodings and the raw bits of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="Y" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$Y$</span>. So in principle we can do it.

But there’s a problem: <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="Y" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$Y$</span> is given to us as a series of bits. That is, we don’t get a vector of the form <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="[2, 6, 11…]" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$[2, 6, 11…]$</span>. We get a vector of the form <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="[0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1…]" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$[0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1…]$</span>, where each bucket of bits (in this example, 4 bits) is a binary-encoding of a number, by convention least-significant-bits first. So we have to somehow re-scale the bits, so that in every cell where we BGG+ multiply some cell <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t_j * Y_{\{i,j,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t_j * Y_{\{i,j,b\}}$</span>, where <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="Y_{\{i,j,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$Y_{\{i,j,b\}}$</span> is the order <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="2^b" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$2^b$</span> bit of the cell <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="Y_{\{i,j\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$Y_{\{i,j\}}$</span>, the encoding that comes out is scaled by <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="2^b" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$2^b$</span>.

For convenience, let’s group together encodings of bits that are of the same order and that will eventually be inside the same value in the answer: that is, the whole column <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t_j * Y_{\{i,j,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t_j * Y_{\{i,j,b\}}$</span> for some specific <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$i$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="b" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$b$</span> across all <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="j" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$j$</span>.

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="\sum_j s * (B_{\{out,i,j,b\}} - t_j * Y_{\{i,j,b\}} * G) + e_{\{out,i,j,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$\sum_j s * (B_{\{out,i,j,b\}} - t_j * Y_{\{i,j,b\}} * G) + e_{\{out,i,j,b\}}$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= s * (B_{\{out,i,b\}} - (tY)_{\{i,b\}} * G) + e_{\{out,i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= s * (B_{\{out,i,b\}} - (tY)_{\{i,b\}} * G) + e_{\{out,i,b\}}$</span>

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

Now we get to the puzzle: how do we combine together bits of different orders?

One naive thing we _could_ do is just rescale and add:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="\sum_{b=0}^{log(q)-1} (s * (B_{\{out,i,b\}} - (tY)_{\{i,b\}} * G) + e_{\{out,i,b\}}) * 2^b" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$\sum_{b=0}^{log(q)-1} (s * (B_{\{out,i,b\}} - (tY)_{\{i,b\}} * G) + e_{\{out,i,b\}}) * 2^b$</span>

The problem with this is that it multiplies up the errors of the high-order digits too much: the error of the highest-order term would get multiplied by <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="2^{log(q)-1} = \frac{q}{2}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$2^{log(q)-1} = \frac{q}{2}$</span> so it would flood the whole range.

So here’s what we do instead:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="\sum_{b=0}^{log(q)-1} (s * (B_{\{out,i,b\}} - (tY)_{\{i,b\}} * G) + e_{\{out,i,b\}}) * G^{-1}(2^bG)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$\sum_{b=0}^{log(q)-1} (s * (B_{\{out,i,b\}} - (tY)_{\{i,b\}} * G) + e_{\{out,i,b\}}) * G^{-1}(2^bG)$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G^{-1}(2^bG)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G^{-1}(2^bG)$</span> is doing all the work here. Basically, this is a ***bucket-wise left shift operator*** *-* it takes each <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="log(q)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$log(q)$</span>\-bit bucket <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="tY" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$tY$</span>, and shifts them all to the left.

Remember, BGG+ encodings are of the form <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * (B - G * m) + e" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * (B - G * m) + e$</span>. And remember that <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G$</span> has this form:

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

This means that BGG+ encodings encode <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span> _simultaneously at every scale_. And what we’re doing here is we’re moving higher-scale encodings of higher-order bits into the first column of each bucket. And because we’re just doing additions and shifts, not multiplications, we avoid the error blowing up by more than the small amount that is introduced by the additions.

To see why <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G^{-1}(2^bG)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G^{-1}(2^bG)$</span> has this shift effect, let’s also look at <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G^{-1}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G^{-1}$</span>. On its own, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G^{-1}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G^{-1}$</span> is the right-inverse of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G$</span>, the *bit decomposition operator* (not a matrix).

Hence, plain <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G^{-1}(G)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G^{-1}(G)$</span> is just the identity matrix:

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

But if we multiply <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G$</span> by <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="2" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$2$</span> before sticking it into <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G^{-1}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G^{-1}$</span>, each binary decomposition is shifted up by one place, and so we get the desired shift:

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

This is just a notational trick that allows the “left-shift every bucket” mechanism to be easily encoded into vector-and-matrix algebra. See also that the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G^{-1}(2^bG)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G^{-1}(2^bG)$</span> matrix is also clearly very low-norm (only ones and zeroes); this is another way to know that this step does not unreasonably blow up error.

The final outcome of this step is that you get a BGG+ encoding of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="tY" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$tY$</span>:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * (B_{\{final,i\}} - G * (tY)_i) + e_{\{final,i\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * (B_{\{final,i\}} - G * (tY)_i) + e_{\{final,i\}}$</span>

Note that these are no longer “normal” encodings, both because the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(tY)_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(tY)_i$</span>’s are full-range values modulo q, and because the evaluator does not know the cleartext values. The evaluator cannot do any further BGG+ multiplication on them. But that’s okay, because they do not have to; the only step the evaluator has left is to remove the “wrapping with <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span>” so that we can get to our final goal, extracting <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(tY)_i + e" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(tY)_i + e$</span>.

To extract <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(tY)_i + e" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(tY)_i + e$</span>, we are going to diverge from BGG+ ABE fully. In ABE, we know that, in those cases where decryption is supposed to be possible, the answer <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="C(tag)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$C(tag)$</span> equals 0. <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G * C(tag)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G * C(tag)$</span> disappears, and that’s exactly why we can extract the message. <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G * C(tag)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G * C(tag)$</span> plays the role of a *blinding factor*. Here, the use case is different: <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(tY)_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(tY)_i$</span> is the entire thing that we want to extract.

Let’s rewrite our BGG+ encoding as:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * B_{\{final,i\}} - s * G * (tY)_i + e_{\{final,i\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * B_{\{final,i\}} - s * G * (tY)_i + e_{\{final,i\}}$</span>

Now, let’s extract a single column from this expression - the lowest-order column in the last bucket.

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * b_i - s * g * (tY)_i + e" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * b_i - s * g * (tY)_i + e$</span>

The choice of lowest-order column diverges from “traditional GSW decryption”, where we extract the highest-order column, but remember: because of our bucket-wise shifting trick, by this point the lowest-order column contains information that was grabbed from the highest-order columns representing the values that we care most about (the message).

We constrain <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> so that its last value (which we’ll denote <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_{last}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_{last}$</span>) equals -1. Also, notice that the column of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G$</span> we chose, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="g" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$g$</span>, is just a bunch of zeroes followed by a 1. Hence, we get a nicely simplified expression:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * b_i - s_{last} * (tY)_i + e_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * b_i - s_{last} * (tY)_i + e_i$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= s * b_i + (tY)_i + e_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= s * b_i + (tY)_i + e_i$</span>

Now, our task is to compute <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * b_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * b_i$</span> so we can remove it.

Let us pull in one fact from a later section: the evaluator has “access” to <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> in the form of an encoded sample <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="ct = (m \otimes s) P_L + e_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$ct = (m \otimes s) P_L + e_L$</span>, where <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span> is the full input to the obfuscated computation and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="\otimes" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$\otimes$</span> is the “tensor product”. That is, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m \otimes s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m \otimes s$</span> is a vector of length <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="len(m) * len(s)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$len(m) * len(s)$</span> that contains <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> multiplied by the first value in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span>, then right after that <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> multiplied by the second value in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span>, and so on. Conveniently, the first value in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span> is fixed to be 1.

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

Now, we use the trapdoor machinery, described in the [ABE section of the previous post](https://vitalik.eth.limo/general/2026/06/29/obfuscation1.html#attribute-based-encryption-abe), to make a low-norm preimage <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_G$</span> that satisfies:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="P_L * K_G = M" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$P_L * K_G = M$</span>

Here, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="M" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$M$</span> is a matrix that contains _all of the_ <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="b_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$b_i$</span>’s - that is, the extracted columns from each <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B_{\{final,i\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B_{\{final,i\}}$</span> matrix - and then is padded with extra zeroes to make the dimensions match up.

This ensures that <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="ct * K_G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$ct * K_G$</span> evaluates to

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="((m \otimes s) * P_L + e_L) * K_G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$((m \otimes s) * P_L + e_L) * K_G$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= (m \otimes s) * P_L * K_G + e_L * K_G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= (m \otimes s) * P_L * K_G + e_L * K_G$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= (m \otimes s) * M + e_g" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= (m \otimes s) * M + e_g$</span>

Now, notice that only the first <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="len(s)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$len(s)$</span> rows of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="M" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$M$</span> are nonzero, and the first <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="len(s)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$len(s)$</span> values in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m \otimes s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m \otimes s$</span> are just <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span>. So the above reduces to:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * M + e_g" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * M + e_g$</span>

Which is a concatenation of all of the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * b_i + e_{\{i,g\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * b_i + e_{\{i,g\}}$</span> that we need.

Now, we can subtract that, and get the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(tY)_i + e_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(tY)_i + e_i$</span> values we need, which are our FHE decryption result. And then finally, the evaluator rounds, to get the final value of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f(x, z)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f(x, z)$</span>.

Here we can once again see where the security comes from: the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_G$</span> “trapdoor” allows the evaluator to extract this *only* for those specific <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="b_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$b_i$</span>, and the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="b_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$b_i$</span> come from <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B_{\{final,i\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B_{\{final,i\}}$</span>, which are bound to the exact shape of the circuit. If the evaluator computes <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * b’_i + e{\{i,g\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * b’_i + e{\{i,g\}}$</span> for some *different* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="b’_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$b’_i$</span>, then they would be left with a <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * (b_i - b’_i)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * (b_i - b’_i)$</span> term blinding the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(tY)_i + e_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(tY)_i + e_i$</span>, and would not be able to extract the answer.

## Adjustments to f(x, z)

It turns out the security of the scheme we described above is only provable under one condition: **that the outputs** <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(tY)_i + e_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(tY)_i + e_i$</span> **are uniformly random** \- in fact, jointly pseudorandom across all <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="2^L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$2^L$</span> inputs. “Jointly pseudorandom” here basically means that if you were given unlimited access to the full exponentially-sized table (though still only polynomial computation time), you would not be able to distinguish it from random data.

This actually makes our work challenging. In a “normal” GSW decryption, the last entry of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t * Y" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t * Y$</span> equals <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="\frac{q}{2} * m + e" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$\frac{q}{2} * m + e$</span>. This would give us two problems:

1. Because the error is almost always much smaller than the message, **the output is very “spiky” around** <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="0" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$0$</span> **and** <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="\frac{q}{2}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$\frac{q}{2}$</span>. Even if the error could somehow always cover the full range (difficult: worst-case and average-case tend to differ massively), LWE error is correlated with the message so it would still leak information
2. **The distribution of outputs** <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span> **is itself not uniform**, because most “natural” functions <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f$</span> are not random.

We can tackle these in turn.

First, we modify the function that we evaluate in FHE. We make <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="z" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$z$</span> contain *two* secrets <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(z_1, z_2)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(z_1, z_2)$</span>: the secret input to the function, and a random PRF key. Then, we do <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="FHE.eval(f’, x, E[z])" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$FHE.eval(f’, x, E[z])$</span>, where:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f’(x, z) = \frac{q}{2} * f(x, z_1) - (\frac{q}{4} - e_{max}) + H_1(x, z_2)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f’(x, z) = \frac{q}{2} * f(x, z_1) - (\frac{q}{4} - e_{max}) + H_1(x, z_2)$</span>

Here, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1$</span> is a hash function that returns values in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="[0 … \frac{q}{2}-2e_{max})" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$[0 … \frac{q}{2}-2e_{max})$</span>, where <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="e_{max}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$e_{max}$</span> is a bound on the largest possible error that our whole procedure could introduce. Formally, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1$</span> must be a PRF (“pseudorandom function”).

For correctness, it’s okay to just think of it as a hash. However, in practice, computing this hash is where almost all of the evaluation time lies, and so making diamond iO practical will almost certainly involve heavily optimizing <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1$</span> to target its specific needs, and not using generic algorithms like SHA256.

In “normal” GSW, the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="\frac{q}{2}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$\frac{q}{2}$</span> factor is implicit - *of course* you multiply the message by <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="\frac{q}{2}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$\frac{q}{2}$</span> because otherwise it might get smudged by the error. Here, we multiply the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f(x, z_1)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f(x, z_1)$</span> part by <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="\frac{q}{2}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$\frac{q}{2}$</span> but not the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1(x, z_2)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1(x, z_2)$</span> part, and we’re okay with a few lower-order digits of that getting mangled by the error - the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1(x, z_2)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1(x, z_2)$</span> is not data we care about recovering, rather it’s meant to be “maximum-range” pseudorandom noise that is there to smudge out the FHE and ABE-related noise. The goal of the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="\frac{q}{4} - e_{max}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$\frac{q}{4} - e_{max}$</span> offset is to “center” the output of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1$</span> (ie. make its range <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="[-(\frac{q}{4} - e_{max}), \frac{q}{4} - e_{max}]" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$[-(\frac{q}{4} - e_{max}), \frac{q}{4} - e_{max}]$</span>), so that you can round to the nearest <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="\frac{q}{2}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$\frac{q}{2}$</span> and then divide to get back <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f(x, z)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f(x, z)$</span>.

Second, we modify the function _again_, by xoring a hash into <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f$</span> itself:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f’(x, z) = \frac{q}{2} * xor(f(x, z_1), H_2(x)) - (\frac{q}{4} - e_{max}) + H_1(x, z_2)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f’(x, z) = \frac{q}{2} * xor(f(x, z_1), H_2(x)) - (\frac{q}{4} - e_{max}) + H_1(x, z_2)$</span>

From <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_2" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_2$</span>, we want a random oracle property. But <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_2" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_2$</span> is not a bottleneck for efficiency, so using generic algorithms like SHA256 is great here.

To get the final output in the clear, we xor <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_2(x)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_2(x)$</span> back out *after* we get the final <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f’(x, z)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f’(x, z)$</span> output from the diamond iO.

The result of this trickery is that <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(tY)_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(tY)_i$</span> is now fully pseudorandom:

* Each highest-order bit is pseudorandom because it gets xor’d with a bit of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_2(x)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_2(x)$</span>, which we assume is pseudorandom (in the formal sense described by the [pseudorandom oracle model](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1204))
* All lower-order bits are generated by <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1(x, z_2)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1(x, z_2)$</span>, which we again assume is pseudorandom. The <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="2e_{max}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$2e_{max}$</span>\-wide empty space between the ranges of possible outputs for the two possible message values is exponentially small compared to <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="q" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$q$</span>, so we can safely ignore it.

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

[This technique](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1742) is sometimes called “PROM bootstrap”, and it is a generic transformation that converts “obfuscation for pseudorandom functionalities” into a more general form of obfuscation that works for any <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f$</span>. Looking at a hash simultaneously as a random oracle and an implementable circuit is also sometimes considered a “sketchy” cryptographic assumption, though it is used widely today, eg. in recursive STARKs.

Finally, if we want to do “traditional” iO, which hides the function, instead of fixing a public function <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f$</span> and hiding a private input <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="z" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$z$</span>, then we do the trick we already did many times in the more conservative forms of obfuscation: make <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f$</span> be a “universal circuit” <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="VM" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$VM$</span> whose private input is a program <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="P" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$P$</span>, and that satisfies <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="VM(x, P) = P(x)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$VM(x, P) = P(x)$</span>.

## How does the evaluator learn the input encodings?

So far, we have just magically assumed that the evaluator gets BGG+ encodings <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * (B_i - G * m_i) + e_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * (B_i - G * m_i) + e_i$</span>. But unfortunately things are not that simple. The obfuscator *could* construct <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="len(m) + L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$len(m) + L$</span> such encodings, for <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_i \in \{0,1\}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_i \in \{0,1\}$</span>, with the same <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> (they would only have to provide both the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="0" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$0$</span> option and the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$1$</span> option for the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="x" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$x$</span> portion of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span>). But this is not secure: if you get two encodings with the same <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B_i$</span> and the same <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> but different <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_i$</span> (if we’re dealing with binary bits, that means <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="0" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$0$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$1$</span>), then you can just subtract them and get <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * G + (e_1 - e_2)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * G + (e_1 - e_2)$</span>, leaking <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> in the clear.

So we have to somehow give the evaluator a gadget that lets them produce encodings for any <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span>, but with a different <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> for each <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span>. Even one bit of change in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span> should completely change the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span>. This is where the core of diamond iO’s machinery comes in.

The trick is as follows. First, remember the structure of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span>: <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="[1, E[z], x, t]" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$[1, E[z], x, t]$</span>. The only thing that changes between different evaluations is <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="x" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$x$</span>.

We will start off with a “base” message, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_0 = [1, E[z], 000…000, t]" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_0 = [1, E[z], 000…000, t]$</span>, and a “base” secret <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_0" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_0$</span>.

For the i’th bit, we will define matrices <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="M_{\{i,0\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$M_{\{i,0\}}$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="M_{\{i,1\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$M_{\{i,1\}}$</span> which are the identity matrix, but with the 1 in the slot corresponding to the i’th bit of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="x" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$x$</span> either deleted or moved to the first row. That is, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="M_{\{i,b_i\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$M_{\{i,b_i\}}$</span> represents the idea “keep <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span> as is, _except_ change the i’th bit in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="x" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$x$</span> to <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="b_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$b_i$</span>”.

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

We also define low-norm matrices <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="S_{\{i,0\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$S_{\{i,0\}}$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="S_{\{i,1\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$S_{\{i,1\}}$</span>, whose goal is to transform the secret.

Hence, any _final_ vector <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_L$</span> can be expressed as <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_0 * M_{\{1,b_1\}} * M_{\{2,b_2\}} * … * M_{\{L,b_L\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_0 * M_{\{1,b_1\}} * M_{\{2,b_2\}} * … * M_{\{L,b_L\}}$</span>. And the corresponding <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_0 * S_{{1,b_1}} * S_{{2,b_2}} * … * S_{{L,b_L}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_0 * S_{{1,b_1}} * S_{{2,b_2}} * … * S_{{L,b_L}}$</span> gives us a unique secret <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_L$</span>. Our goal will be to “fuse” these transformations together, so that for each specific <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_L$</span> you generate, you get BGG+ encodings constructed with a unique corresponding secret <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_L$</span>.

We will “fuse” these vectors and matrices by tensoring them together, and then wrapping them in encodings so that they cannot be unpacked.

A mini example - we’ll start with tensoring the vectors <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span>:

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

The leftmost value in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span> is constrained to equal <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$1$</span>, and the rightmost value in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> is constrained to equal <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="-1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$-1$</span>.

And now this is what tensoring matrices looks like (all un-written entries are zeroes):

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

See how <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="M" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$M$</span> is in the shape we described above, and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="S" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$S$</span> is constrained so that it doesn’t touch the last column, keeping the last value of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> at -1.

A key property of tensoring is that if <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_1 = m_0 * M_{\{1, b_1\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_1 = m_0 * M_{\{1, b_1\}}$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_1 = s_0 * S_{\{1, b_1\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_1 = s_0 * S_{\{1, b_1\}}$</span>, then <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(m_1 \otimes s_1) = (m_0 \otimes s_0) * (M_{\{1, b_1\}} \otimes S_{\{1, b_1\}})" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(m_1 \otimes s_1) = (m_0 \otimes s_0) * (M_{\{1, b_1\}} \otimes S_{\{1, b_1\}})$</span>. For convenience, we’ll define <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="Q_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$Q_{\{i,b\}}$</span> as equaling <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(M_{\{i, b\}} \otimes S_{\{i, b\}})" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(M_{\{i, b\}} \otimes S_{\{i, b\}})$</span>

So far, the evaluator’s formula is: start with <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="q_0 = m_0 \otimes s_0" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$q_0 = m_0 \otimes s_0$</span>, multiply by each <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="Q_{\{i, b_i\}} =M_{\{i, b_i\}} \otimes S_{\{i, b_i\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$Q_{\{i, b_i\}} =M_{\{i, b_i\}} \otimes S_{\{i, b_i\}}$</span> in sequence, and then get <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="q_L = m_L \otimes s_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$q_L = m_L \otimes s_L$</span> at the end.

We have already gotten somewhere: we now have a way to generate *some kind of encoding* of each possible <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_L$</span> that the evaluator might need, such that it’s bound to a unique <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_L$</span>. The problem: so far, this encoding exposes <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_L$</span> (including the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t$</span> bits which the evaluator is not meant to know) and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_L$</span> completely in the clear.

The next step will be multiplying in matrices in the right places to “blind” these encodings at each step.

The obfuscator will give the evaluator an encoding <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="p_0 ​=q_0​ * P_0 ​+ e_0" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$p_0 ​=q_0​ * P_0 ​+ e_0$</span>

The obfuscator will then generate low-norm matrices <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_{\{i,b\}}$</span>, which satisfy <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="P_{i-1} * K_{\{i,b\}} =  Q_{\{i,b\}} * P_i + E_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$P_{i-1} * K_{\{i,b\}} =  Q_{\{i,b\}} * P_i + E_{\{i,b\}}$</span>. This is allowed, again, because of the trapdoor mechanism.

The evaluator can then walk down the exponentially-sized tree of possible encodings. Here’s what this tree looks like graphically. Notice that even though the tree is of size <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="2^L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$2^L$</span>, the number of actually-distinct “edge matrices” that generate this whole tree is only <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="2L+1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$2L+1$</span>, including the final <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_f$</span> that we’ll get to later).

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

And here’s why this works mathematically:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="p_1 = p_0 * K_{\{1,b_1\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$p_1 = p_0 * K_{\{1,b_1\}}$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= q_0 * P_0 * K_{\{1,b_1\}} + e_0 * K_{\{1,b_1\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= q_0 * P_0 * K_{\{1,b_1\}} + e_0 * K_{\{1,b_1\}}$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * P_1 + e_0 * K_{\{1,b_1\}} + q_0 * E_{\{1,b_1\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * P_1 + e_0 * K_{\{1,b_1\}} + q_0 * E_{\{1,b_1\}}$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * P_1 + e_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * P_1 + e_1$</span>

And then:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="p_2 = p_1 * K_{\{2,b_2\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$p_2 = p_1 * K_{\{2,b_2\}}$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * P_1 * K_{\{2,b_2\}} + e_1 * K_{\{2,b_2\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * P_1 * K_{\{2,b_2\}} + e_1 * K_{\{2,b_2\}}$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * Q_{\{2,b_2\}} * P_2 + e_1 * K_{\{2,b_2\}} + q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * E_{\{2,b_2\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * Q_{\{2,b_2\}} * P_2 + e_1 * K_{\{2,b_2\}} + q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * E_{\{2,b_2\}}$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * Q_{{2,b_2}} * P_2  + e_2" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * Q_{{2,b_2}} * P_2  + e_2$</span>

And so on all the way up until <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="p_L = q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * … * Q_{\{L,b_L\}} * P_L + e_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$p_L = q_0 * Q_{\{1,b_1\}} * … * Q_{\{L,b_L\}} * P_L + e_L$</span>, where <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="q_0 * Q_{{1,b_1}} * … * Q_{{L,b_L}} = q_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$q_0 * Q_{{1,b_1}} * … * Q_{{L,b_L}} = q_L$</span>.

Notice <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="e_{i-1} * K_{\{i,b_i\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$e_{i-1} * K_{\{i,b_i\}}$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="q_{i-1} * E_{{i,b_i}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$q_{i-1} * E_{{i,b_i}}$</span> both collapse into <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="e_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$e_i$</span>. This means that <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_{\{i,b\}}$</span>, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="Q_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$Q_{\{i,b\}}$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="q" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$q$</span> (and hence <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span>, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span>, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="M_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$M_{\{i,b\}}$</span>, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="S_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$S_{\{i,b\}}$</span>) all have to be low-norm (and they are).

Now, we have an actually-blinded encoding of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="q_L = m_L \otimes s_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$q_L = m_L \otimes s_L$</span>. But it’s not quite the right format. We have:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(m_L \otimes s_L) * P_L + e_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(m_L \otimes s_L) * P_L + e_L$</span>

We need:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_L * (B_i - G * m_L[i]) + e_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_L * (B_i - G * m_L[i]) + e_i$</span>

To cross this bridge, we add _another_ trapdoor <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_f$</span>. It needs to satisfy:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="P_L * K_f = u_1 \otimes B_{full} - I \otimes G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$P_L * K_f = u_1 \otimes B_{full} - I \otimes G$</span>

Here we just introduced a few pieces of new notation, so let’s go through them:

* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="u_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$u_1$</span> is a vector that is 1 in the first position and 0 everywhere else. Depending on context, it means “select the first (column / row / bucket / entry)”
* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B_{full}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B_{full}$</span> is the concatenation of the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B$</span> matrices for the encodings of the whole input: <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B_i$</span> as in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * (B_i - G * m_i) + e_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * (B_i - G * m_i) + e_i$</span>
* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="u_1 \otimes B_{full}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$u_1 \otimes B_{full}$</span> means “vertically stack many copies of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B_{full}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B_{full}$</span> where the first is multiplied by 1 and the rest multiplied by 0” - or in even simpler terms, put a bunch of zeroes below <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B_{full}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B_{full}$</span>
* <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="I \otimes G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$I \otimes G$</span> looks like many copies of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G$</span> along a diagonal; it means “multiply by <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G$</span> bucket-wise”

Also notice that here (like the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_G$</span> case, *unlike* the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_{\{i,b\}}$</span> case), there is no error on the right side; that is fine, because the error in the final ciphertexts will come from elsewhere, and the value on the right is a public expression, so there is no security risk to not masking it.

Now, let’s see what happens if we multiply <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(m_L \otimes s_L) * P_L + e_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(m_L \otimes s_L) * P_L + e_L$</span> by <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_f$</span>:

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="((m_L \otimes s_L) * P_L + e_L) * K_f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$((m_L \otimes s_L) * P_L + e_L) * K_f$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= (m_L \otimes s_L) * P_L * K_f + e_L * K_f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= (m_L \otimes s_L) * P_L * K_f + e_L * K_f$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= (m_L \otimes s_L) * u_1 \otimes B_{full} - (m_L \otimes s_L) * (I \otimes G) + e_f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= (m_L \otimes s_L) * u_1 \otimes B_{full} - (m_L \otimes s_L) * (I \otimes G) + e_f$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= s_L * B_{full} - (m_L \otimes s_L) * (I \otimes G) + e_f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= s_L * B_{full} - (m_L \otimes s_L) * (I \otimes G) + e_f$</span>

<span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="= s_L * B_{full} - m_L \otimes (s_L * G) + e_f" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$= s_L * B_{full} - m_L \otimes (s_L * G) + e_f$</span>

The last two lines are the most nonobvious. What’s going on is: because <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_L$</span> (like all message vectors) starts with 1, the first bucket of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_L \otimes s_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_L \otimes s_L$</span> is just <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_L$</span>. And on the other hand, below the first bucket of rows, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="u_1 \otimes B_{full}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$u_1 \otimes B_{full}$</span> just equals zero. Hence, <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(m_L \otimes s_L) * (u_1 \otimes B_{full})" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(m_L \otimes s_L) * (u_1 \otimes B_{full})$</span> just reduces to <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_L * B_{full}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_L * B_{full}$</span>. And then the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="I \otimes G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$I \otimes G$</span> plays its role as many copies of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="G" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$G$</span> that all get multiplied by many copies of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span>, one for each message value in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m_L$</span>.

(In the paper, they split up <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B_{full}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B_{full}$</span> into <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B_{att}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B_{att}$</span> (excluding <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t$</span> in the inputs) and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B_t" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B_t$</span>, and run the above procedure on those two pieces separately. This is mathematically equivalent to what was described here. The conceptual reason to separate is that they are different kinds of data - the raw values of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="[1, E[z], x]" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$[1, E[z], x]$</span> are given to the evaluator, but the raw values in <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t$</span> are not)

<center><br>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

</center><br>

And the output is literally just the concatenation of all the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_L * (B_i - G * m_L[i]) + e_{\{f,i\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_L * (B_i - G * m_L[i]) + e_{\{f,i\}}$</span> BGG+ encodings that we need.

## Re-summarizing diamond iO

* The evaluator gets <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="p_0" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$p_0$</span>, which is an encoding of (i) <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span> with the function-input parts set to zero and (ii) an initial key <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_0" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_0$</span> tensored together
* For each bit of the message, the evaluator can choose either <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_{i,0}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_{i,0}$</span> or <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_{i,1}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_{i,1}$</span>, which play the role of simultaneously (i) writing either 0 or 1 in as the i’th bit of the function-input part of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span>, and (ii) mixing in a new factor into the key
* At the end, we have <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="p_L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$p_L$</span> which encode the final <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="m" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$m$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> tensored together. We multiply by another trapdoor to push things into the final form: BGG+ encodings of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="[1, E[z], x, t]" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$[1, E[z], x, t]$</span>
* The evaluator then does the BGG+ computation to compute the ciphertext of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f’(x, z) = \frac{q}{2} * xor(f(x, z_1), H_2(x)) - (\frac{q}{4} - e_{max}) + H_1(x, z_2)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f’(x, z) = \frac{q}{2} * xor(f(x, z_1), H_2(x)) - (\frac{q}{4} - e_{max}) + H_1(x, z_2)$</span>
* Decrypting a GSW ciphertext is “just” vector-by-matrix multiplying <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t * Y" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t * Y$</span> and then rounding. Here, we have the bits of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="Y" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$Y$</span>, both as BGG+ encodings and as cleartext, and we have just the BGG+ encodings (no cleartext) of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t$</span>.
* The evaluator does this as a BGG+ multiplication, but with a bucket-wise left shift operation to appropriately scale entries of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="t*Y" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$t*Y$</span> that represent high-order bits
* This gives the evaluator an encoding <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * B_{\{final,i\}} - s * G * (tY)_i + e_{\{final,i\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * B_{\{final,i\}} - s * G * (tY)_i + e_{\{final,i\}}$</span>
* The evaluator extracts a single column - the lowest-order entry in the bucket corresponding to the last entry of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s$</span> (which is fixed to -1). This lets us simplify to <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * b_i + (tY)_i + e_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * b_i + (tY)_i + e_i$</span>
* Finally, the evaluator has a “trapdoor matrix” which allows computing all <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * b_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * b_i$</span> at the same time - but only for those specific <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="b_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$b_i$</span>. This lets them subtract <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s * b_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s * b_i$</span> out, and just have <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="(tY)_i + e_i" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$(tY)_i + e_i$</span>
* The evaluator then rounds-and-divides this, and xors back <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_2(x)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_2(x)$</span> in the clear, to get the desired result <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="f(x, z)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$f(x, z)$</span>

## Security

The most “controversial” part of this protocol is the mechanism for generating the BGG+ encodings for the input. This relies on two fairly new cryptographic assumptions, called _all-product LWE_ and _evasive LWE_. Evasive LWE was introduced in [Wee22](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/906); all-product LWE is unique to diamond iO.

* **Evasive LWE** says that it’s safe to publish pre-images of a secret-bearing target. Roughly, if you have two matrices <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="A" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$A$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="C" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$C$</span>, and samples <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="sA + e_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$sA + e_1$</span> and <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="sC + e_2" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$sC + e_2$</span> (both errors independent) that are indistinguishable from random, then publishing a low-norm preimage <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B$</span> satisfying <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="A * B = C" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$A * B = C$</span> won’t make the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="sA + e_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$sA + e_1$</span> samples distinguishable from random. Note in particular that publishing <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="B" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$B$</span> allows an adversary to convert <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="sA + e_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$sA + e_1$</span> samples into <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="sC + e_1B" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$sC + e_1B$</span>; the assumption says that this is safe. In our case, the assumption implies that the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_{\{i,b\}}$</span> are safe to publish, despite the fact that they are pre-images of a masked but secret-bearing target: <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="P_{i-1} * K_{\{i,b\}} = C" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$P_{i-1} * K_{\{i,b\}} = C$</span> where <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="C = Q_{\{i,b\}} * P_i + E_{\{i,b\}} = (M_{\{i,b\}} \otimes S_{\{i,b\}}) * P_i + E_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$C = Q_{\{i,b\}} * P_i + E_{\{i,b\}} = (M_{\{i,b\}} \otimes S_{\{i,b\}}) * P_i + E_{\{i,b\}}$</span>, where the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="S_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$S_{\{i,b\}}$</span> are the building blocks of the secret.
* **All-product LWE** says that the family of all <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="s_x (B - x \otimes G) + e_x" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$s_x (B - x \otimes G) + e_x$</span>, across all <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="2^L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$2^L$</span> values of x, with secrets constructed via the *path-product* mechanism we described above, is jointly pseudorandom. That is, *this particular way* of constructing many LWE samples with many secrets is safe, as safe as if all <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="2^L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$2^L$</span> secrets were truly independent. Note that this assumes that the initial errors entering the product are pseudorandom; in the diamond iO use case, because we published the <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="K_{\{i,b\}}" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$K_{\{i,b\}}$</span> matrices, we can only assume *that* if we also accept the evasive LWE assumption.

These LWE assumptions are at the same time plausible, avoiding many pitfalls that we have come to understand from a decade of attempts to create novel LWE assumptions that ended up broken by “zeroizing” attacks, but also novel and risky. Evasive LWE is non-falsifiable [in Naor’s sense](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-45146-4_6): formally, it says “for every algorithm that can distinguish X there exists an algorithm that can distinguish Y…” so it’s hard to tell if you even have a counterexample. There are already known classes of situations in which evasive LWE is false; diamond iO deliberately chooses a type of evasive LWE assumption that avoids this.

More security analysis is needed to verify that these assumptions are safe.

## Efficiency

Constructing the BGG+ encodings is relatively “easy” (in part because you can actually use a fan-out greater than 2, eg. a fan-out of 256 fills in 8 bits of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="x" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$x$</span> per multiplication). The hard part is the BGG+ evaluation, which has “ABE * FHE” overhead, where the FHE is itself GSW, which nobody uses in production because it’s far less efficient than more mainstream algorithms like BFV. GSW is needed because it has “nice” algebraic properties, including no need for relinearization or key-switching, and the ability to put plaintext into any size bits of the ciphertext.

On top of this, there are other sources of inefficiency and limitation:

* The whole mechanism also only tolerates low-depth circuits, because the error blows up a lot with each round of BGG+ evaluation *and* with each bit added to the input (we casually papered over this in the explanations by implicitly invoking a “low-norm * low-norm = low-norm” argument, but over many layers, it adds up).
* As with all forms of obfuscation so far, the need to “walk over” <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="2^L" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$2^L$</span> possible inputs inside the proof means that the system requires “subexponentially secure” parameters, which are much larger than normal.

The main *concrete* bottleneck is actually computation of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1(x, z)" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1(x, z)$</span> inside of the ABE * FHE. The main contributor to cost is depth (as depth increases the dimensions needed to handle the error). If the computation itself is deep, there are ways to “refresh” noise for BGG+ encodings, but these methods themselves depend on having a feasible <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1$</span>. Hence, depth of <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1$</span> is the concrete bottleneck. Diamond iO currently uses a “tree” of [Goldreich PRG executions](https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~oded/PDF/prg10.pdf) to instantiate <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1$</span>. This has multiplicative depth 3 per fan-out, and the number of fan-outs required is proportional to the input length.

These reasons are why, in the chart showing different types of obfuscation at the start of this post, diamond iO lands in the “very aggressive” and “planetary” point of the chart.

If we want to improve concrete efficiency of diamond iO, a few possible paths come to mind:

* Replace the tree of Goldreich PRG instantiations with something more efficient
* Find some way to remove <span data-type="inlineMath" data-latex="H_1" data-display="no" data-evaluate="no">$H_1$</span> completely. Perhaps this could involve moving the noise generation into the input encoding step, though [there are known attacks](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/1085) against such constructions.
* Replace the GSW with some more efficient FHE - either something BGV / CKKS flavor, or [packed GSW](https://security-kouza.github.io/paper/IEICE2016_hiromasa.pdf) (see also: [my exploration here](https://github.com/vbuterin/crazy_gsw)), and figure out how to make the conditional decryption work there
* Find some way to at least partially “collapse” the ABE and FHE layers together. Maybe this means modifying BGG+ to embrace the fact that FHE operates “natively” over approximate computation
* Find a way to remove the “subexponentially secure” requirement on the proof side
* Find some optimizations that much more explicitly engineer around solely trying to obfuscate the “iO-complete program” (decrypt an FHE ciphertext only if you receive a valid STARK proving that it was constructed by FHE-evaluating the right circuit on valid inputs), which you can then use to obfuscate anything else

A key advantage of diamond iO is its friendliness to analysis, because of its simplicity. There are no towers of “protocols inside protocols inside protocols” like in more conservative obfuscation variants - the only nesting is the FHE inside of ABE. It can be understood without reference to the entire tower of constructions invented over the past 20 years by cryptographers: you don’t need sublinear randomized encodings, functional encryption, garbled circuits, split FHE or even full ABE (we’re using the core machinery of BGG+, but the details are sufficiently different that the advantage to someone who already knows how it works is much lower). For these reasons, I hope that diamond iO can get much more attention and analysis on both security and optimization, and we can get to an obfuscation protocol that we can actually run.
